one_liner: Research codec for 8/16-bit multivariate integer time series; beats Simple8b, FastPFor and SIMD-BP128 on ratio at GB/s decode.
what_it_does: Lossless compressor for quantized sensor time series stored as row-major uint8_t or uint16_t samples with up to thousands of channels. The API is four C-style function pairs (sprintz_compress_delta_8b / sprintz_compress_xff_8b and the 16-bit versions, plus matching decompress calls) that take a source pointer, length and ndims and write a self-describing 8-byte header plus packed data into a caller-supplied buffer. It is not a drop-in for an integer codec on uint32 posting lists: inputs must already be 8- or 16-bit integers.
how_it_is_fast: Each sample is predicted from earlier samples (plain delta, or FIRE, a per-channel online-learned autoregressive filter updated with downsampled sign gradients), and the zigzag-encoded residuals of 8-row blocks are bit-packed per channel with a 3- or 4-bit width header; all-zero blocks become runs (15-bit run counter), so sparse or constant data collapses. Packing uses BMI2 pext/pdep and decode is AVX2 (_mm256 zigzag decode, prediction and prefix-add across 32 channels per vector), with state of a few bytes per channel. The paper adds an optional Huffman stage for higher ratio (search snippet only; paper blocked).
when_to_use: IoT or wearable sensor streams already quantized to 8 or 16 bits, many channels sampled together, where you want ratio near general-purpose codecs and multi-GB/s single-thread decode.
Small blocks (1 KB to 10 KB) on memory-constrained nodes, where the README's extra figures show Sprintz gaining relative to other codecs.
Smooth or slowly drifting signals where delta or FIRE prediction leaves small residuals, and long flat stretches that the zero-block RLE removes.
As a research baseline when evaluating time-series codecs, using the author's lzbench fork for comparable runs.
when_not_to_use: Sorted 32/64-bit integer lists (posting lists, IDs): only 8- and 16-bit element types exist; use FastPFor, simdcomp or TurboPFor there.
Non-x86 targets: sprintz_xff.h static_asserts __AVX2__ and bitpack.h includes immintrin.h for pext/pdep; issue #6 (2024, open) reports it fails to build on Apple M2.
Untrusted or possibly corrupt input: decompress takes no source length or destination capacity and trusts the header's ngroups and ndims.

Production use that needs a maintained library: last commit 2021-01-10, six open issues unanswered, no build system other than an Xcode project and the lzbench fork's Makefile, and issue #3 reports the paper's speeds could not be reproduced.

integration.dependencies: none for the codec (AVX2 and BMI2 intrinsics); benchmarks need the separate dblalock/lzbench fork plus Python, joblib, pandas, seaborn
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (lzbench fork builds it with -std=c++0x -O3 -march=native); README says only tested with Clang on OS X; issue #2 reports Clang errors 'object backing the pointer will be destroyed at the end of the full-expression'
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 and BMI2 only
integration.thread_safety: not documented; functions keep no global mutable state beyond static const tables and allocate scratch per call, so separate calls on separate buffers look independent

gotchas: Compressor leaks memory on every call: compress_rowmajor_xff_rle callocs header_bytes and coef_counters_ar and never frees them (only stripe_* arrays and errs are freed), so long-running encoders grow without bound.

No output-size bound or capacity argument: the encoder comments that its memset 'can overrun dest buff', and the AVX2 decoder writes whole 32-byte vectors, so size destination buffers with slack; the needed slack is not documented.
Every call mallocs and frees scratch arrays, which costs time on small blocks; the README's GB/s figure comes from lzbench runs on large buffers.
Source files carry 'Copyright 2017 D Blalock. All rights reserved.' headers while the repository LICENSE is Apache-2.0; the LICENSE file governs, but keep it with any vendored copy.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Sprintz over FastPFor, simdcomp or TurboPFor only for multichannel 8/16-bit sensor time series, where its prediction plus per-channel packing exploits correlation in time that those uint32 codecs ignore (the README notes they reach almost no compression on unpadded bytes); for sorted 32-bit lists or any non-x86 target, those siblings (or Stream VByte for varint-style data) are the safer choice.
verified_claims_summary: The IMWUT 2018 paper and README compare Sprintz with Simple8b, FastPFor and SIMD-BP128 (fed 8/16-bit data zero-padded to 32 bits, ratios divided by the padding factor) and with LZ4, Zstd-class codecs on AMPDs, MSRC-12, PAMAP, UCI Gas and UCR datasets via the author's lzbench fork, reporting top compression ratios and single-thread decompression above 3 GB/s (paper abstract, search snippet only). The fork's Makefile builds with -O3 -march=native; the CPU model is not given on any page reachable here, and one user (issue #3) could not reproduce the speeds.
status_note: Abandoned research code since 2021-01-10 with no maintainer replies to six open issues; Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor, but plan to fix the encoder leak and add bounds checks yourself.
